speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head R of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There has been a good take-up rate for this service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The feedback on these services is also good, averaging four out of five stars in the post-usage surveys.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This achievement comes on top of other initiatives such as the operationalisation of the Protection from Harassment Court with simplified processes allowing a person to navigate the system on his own without the need for a lawyer, and the Apostille Act which was put into effect on 16 September 2021 which helped Singapore travellers easily get Apostilles for their Singapore-issued vaccination records for travel to countries, if so required, as a condition of entry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These and other moves have enhanced access to justice and make our legal system more efficient and trusted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have two suggestions that I hope the Minister would consider to strengthen this even more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the simplification of the probate and administration process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have been advocating for change in this process, especially for non-contentious matters, for sometime now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggested the Japanese Kobeki system, which does not involve the courts, to be looked at.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The vast majority of probate and administration cases are simple.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, the current system requiring executors or administrators to file applications in Court is cumbersome and costly, as it involves lawyers in a Rube Goldberg machine or process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several years back, the Government agreed to look at my proposal to simplify the system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Means testing is an important part of prudence in public spending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Balanced against prudence is the assurance that cost will not be an obstacle to access to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that in the past five years, the total number of applications has dropped.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Between 2017 and 2019, these applications generally numbered around the 9,000s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2020, the number went down to 7,722.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2021, it went down further, to 6,651.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that the number of successful applicants has also gone down.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Between 2017 and 2019, the average number of successful applicants is 6,180.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For 2020, it went down to 5,466; and in 2021, it went down even further to 4,928.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The percentage of unsuccessful applications that did not satisfy the means test criteria is about 80%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This could mean that many well-to-do people are trying their luck.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But looking at the benchmarks for income in the other parts of our policies on means-testing, I do not think so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, in comparison a person under the Joint Single Scheme (JSS) may apply for a public rental flat from HDB, if his gross monthly salary does not exceed $1,500.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end though, two withdrew, leaving only three applicants to proceed with their applications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, this is too small a number, given the demand for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also checked the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) website and noted the reference to this statutory discretion is respectfully rather cursory.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I was not able to find a reference to the Means Test Panel and the fact that the decisions of the panel can be appealed to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The illustrations as to what constitutes "just and proper" circumstances are also rather limited.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From time to time, our laws have to be updated in keeping with developments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could please outline his plans in this area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would also like to make two proposals for his kind consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I propose that the Ministry look at amending the Limitation Act 1959 to address a recent decision of the Court of Appeal to the effect that claims in unjust enrichment and restitution for wrongs are not covered under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, stale claims based on these causes of action be potentially be brought in our Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I propose that the Ministry review the merits of retaining the provisions of the Debtors Act 1934, which allows for judgment debtors to be committed to civil prison after an examination before a Court on the inability to pay or satisfy the judgment debt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, this provision is anachronistic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It has not being used, as I have been told, since 2013, pursuant to a response to my Parliamentary Question recently.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is tending to the cost of supply.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, we must look at demand for legal services and ensure access to justice for all.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, disputes are often an unpleasant but inevitable by-product of our personal and work life interactions and also in the course of doing business.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If unresolved, some of these disputes end up in litigation before the civil Courts or for resolution before Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To those of us who have had the unfortunate need to go through litigation or dispute resolution, we know that it is not only resource intensive but also likely to be a frustrating and trying experience.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But on the other hand, even if one navigates successfully through the process and obtains a favourable judgment or order, it does not mean that the problem or the dispute is resolved instantly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If, for whatever reason, a party does not comply with the judgment or order, the other party will then have no choice but to take steps to enforce it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The enforcement process is equally, if not more, painful.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When workers face issues with an employer and get judgments from the Courts or the Employment Claims Tribunal that they are not satisfied with, they would still need to be enforced in the same manner as an order made by the Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This would involve going through an entire rigmarole of processes set out in the rules of Court pertaining to the filing of relevant forms, documents, as well as the payment of Court fees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In most instances, they would still need to engage a lawyer and may sometimes still be subjected to a protracted enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, access to justice is an important issue and in recent times, MinLaw and the Singapore Courts have taken important steps to make sure that those who need to access the legal system are able to get it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes making proceedings easier for the self-represented, the expansion of legal aid by easing the means test and providing funding for some criminal legal aid cases too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is also considering a fully funded public defender’s office.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the last year, the Ministry has also permitted the use of third-party funding and conditional fee arrangements for arbitrations, as well as for proceedings before the Singapore International Commercial Courts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a helpful development that levels the playing field somewhat, between local and international law firms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, one area where I still believe more can be done is in the area of domestic litigation for those who do not qualify for legal aid, but who may still lack the resources for an expensive, longdrawn suit, even if they have a valid claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In these types of situations, I have two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means they can collect a proportion of any damages recovered.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The country with the most liberal system in relation to the above is probably the US and, despite the potentially high legal costs there, access to justice is rarely a complaint by civil litigants because if a person has a good case, it is usually possible to find a lawyer to take it up and share the risk.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UK as well now allows both, although it circumscribes limits to the proportion of damages that can be claimed in certain situations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main concern cited against this is the risk of frivolous lawsuits and that the advocate, by taking an interest in the litigation, may not be able to perform his duty as an officer of the Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the risk of frivolous lawsuits, I think this is unlikely to be high because lawyers will be bearing the risk and it will be a big investment for them as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to lawyers acting as professionals, I think this risk can be managed and other countries, such as the US and the UK, are able to function with this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a melting pot and our legal system currently provides a robust and clear framework for foreign judgments to be enforced here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One area though, where this is not so easily enforceable, is in the case of matrimonial law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And we are also a melting pot for mixed marriages, where 25% of Singaporeans marry spouses of a different nationality and we have lots of foreign marriages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, it is not automatically easy to enforce custody orders or maintenance orders from a foreign court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These have to still be enforced under first principles through the Guardianship of Infants Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I would be grateful if the Ministry could consider making it easier to enforce maintenance and custody orders from foreign courts, especially if divorce proceedings are determined there.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The spouse can be a litigant-in-person who finds the legal system complex and difficult to navigate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Residents struggling to make ends meet, single parent, single income, looking after elderly grandparents and the children at the same time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One Clementi resident shared about her journey as a litigant-in-person.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She had to navigate the various intermediaries – VITAL, which is a department under MOF, as well as CrimsonLogic – an entity that apparently handles some of the payment transactions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In February 2021, a Singapore Academy of Law blog, in an excerpt of a book by NUS professors Jaclyn Neo and Helena Whalen-Bridge stated, and I quote: "The legal system itself may limit the litigant-in-person’s access to justice, particularly in terms of equality of access, due to complex procedural rules".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Despite this, some spouses still proceed to deal as a litigant-in-person for divorce proceedings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has MinLaw studied why and done a deep dive into this issue?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the system be streamlined for litigants-in-person of limited means?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is MinLaw considering additional enforcement mechanisms against errant spouses who do not attend or comply with maintenance orders and timely payments because justice delayed is justice denied?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Besides this, what other efforts have been made to increase public awareness among beneficiaries and reduce the amount of unclaimed CPF monies held by the Public Trustee?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Further, the probate and administration process in Court for beneficiaries can be quite cumbersome to navigate before they are able to appoint the executor and administrator of the estate of the deceased.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Hence, may I know what are MinLaw's plans to make it easier during the probate process for beneficiaries to appoint executors and administrators particularly for those with limited means or those without any legal representation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Technology is becoming increasingly an important element in the practice and business of law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My own firm, which is part of a larger international set-up, has a global collaborative platform focused on developing, deploying and investing in new technologies in the practice of law in our offices all around the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: It is almost imperative nowadays to incorporate and leverage technology in legal practice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Clients are increasingly looking for quicker assistance and more are specifically seeking out innovative solutions and the adoption of technology.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, how is MinLaw supporting law practices in their digitalisation journey and also to encourage legal practitioners to utilise legal technology in their practice?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is especially so for smaller or local firms which may not have the benefit of economies of scale when seeking to acquire such legal technology solutions on their own.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Chief Justice was quoted in a Yahoo!

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: News article on Monday as saying this at a recent Court of Three Judges hearing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is because the stakes are so high.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It takes a certain dedication to be in a profession that, amongst other things, defends life and liberty, that acts for commercial interests that may have wide-ranging consequences, that challenges in Court the constitutionality of laws made in this House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many suggestions have been made by various people and I would like to add three.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a graduate law student myself – my first degree was in political science and I took up a law degree only after working a few years in the Civil Service – I can attest that once someone makes that sacrifice of three years with no salary or advancement to obtain a law degree, they will likely remain in the profession, as most of my batch have.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it was recently suggested to me by a Senior Counsel that the current training contract scheme has lost the emotional elements of the previous pupillage system, which created a bond between new lawyers and their pupil master, and to the profession.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Gone also are the formal dinners that trainee lawyers were invited to attend, where they would be seated with and would get to know senior practitioners.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These unique and iconic traditions of the profession helped to build camaraderie and fraternity and gave life to the idea of being part of an ancient and noble profession.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even in the UK, from which we inherit our legal traditions, the importance of these "dining-in sessions" was recently affirmed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, while stress from the job is inevitable, stress from bosses and from the working environment is not.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that modules on leadership and management have recently been added to the compulsory training for lawyers becoming partners.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is merit in considering including these types of courses as compulsory modules in the Continuing Professional Development programme for middle and senior category lawyers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, Singapore's position as a global legal hub is well-known and one that we do not take for granted.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But every system is, ultimately, made up of people and around the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is no exception and we have heard instances of young lawyers leaving the industry and feeling disillusioned.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The demands of practice today, with unrelenting advances of technology, long hours, complex cases and transactions, are very real.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it sounds like an exciting career, it is one that, more often than not, veers towards burnout and, if we do not do something meaningfully to tackle structural and attitudinal factors, it will be an unhealthy race to the bottom.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, the legal needs of our society and economy are constantly evolving.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To remain as a preferred jurisdiction for dispute resolution, we must remain competitive and have good people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any structural or skilling concerns to ensure that we can continue to meet the evolving legal needs of our society and economy?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, may I take all my five cuts together, please?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: First, allow me to declare that I am a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Technological advancements have made the arrangement and management of case documents easier.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Additionally, clients' needs have evolved as they themselves face increasingly complex issues because of technological advances and cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MinLaw equipping the legal profession to better meet the evolving legal needs of our society and economy?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, while law graduates emerging into the industry would be the most up to date, legal practitioners who have spent many years in the field and have already honed their craft might find the challenge of incorporating technological advances far too steep.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MinLaw supporting the law practices in their digitalisation journey?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Whether through arbitration, mediation or some other form of dispute resolution, Singapore is known to be even-handed and fair and transparent in its dealings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This has been built upon the backbone of creating and continually updating our law and regulations and developing the relevant infrastructure to take on the flow of legal work through our borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Additionally, we have cultivated local legal talent to become world-class arbitrators, mediators and advocates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, the pandemic has moved many dispute resolutions online and the places having the most updated technology and best handling of the pandemic become the destinations best suited for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What plans does MinLaw have to maintain Singapore's position as an international dispute resolution hub today?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With the world increasingly interconnected and businesses and revenue going wherever there is the greatest protection over assets and the best environment for innovation, Singapore needs to keep pace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Having the required legal regime and infrastructure will allow for greater foreign investment into local enterprises and allow for the growth of local enterprises to explore and lead the way in blockchain and other cutting-edge developments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How has MinLaw been supporting the local enterprises in the area of IP to build infrastructure as well as to monetise their IP?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Over the years, the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) has done very well to convert under-utilised state land into community spaces, such as parks and even quarantine facilities during the peak of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, by partnering the community in engaging the public to receive feedback on how state properties can be retrofitted and adapted, we can continue to create a beautiful Singapore and maximise the usage of our land.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does MinLaw plan to continually repurpose and rejuvenate state properties to breathe new life into them?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The range of issues raised in Members' cuts reflect the extensive and diverse reach of our legal system and its fundamental importance to Singapore, as well as the rapidly-evolving landscape that we are navigating.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As we adjust to living with COVID-19, we will pay renewed attention to strengthening the rule of law and access to justice and, of course, at the same time, keeping an eye on being able to seize the opportunities ahead of us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will secure our place in a post-COVID-19 world and ensure that we continue to thrive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In support of this, my Ministry remains focused on three broad areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, building a legal system that is trusted, effective and accessible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, strengthening Singapore as a legal services and intellectual property hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And third, enhancing our management of state land and properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will address in response to the cuts along these themes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore has a legal system renowned for efficiency, effectiveness and fairness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are not, however, resting on our laurels and will continue to make improvements across various facets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will promote affordability, timeliness, simplicity and, of course, effectiveness and trust, as Mr Murali Pillai puts it, for all litigants – key characteristics of a country with a strong rule of law and good governance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An important aspect of a strong rule of law is to ensure that Court judgments are efficiently enforced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked about the enforcement of Court orders following prolonged litigation, often requiring further time and resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also received feedback that the time, effort and costs of enforcing a judgment in some cases, particularly where there is a lower-value judgment, can be disproportionate to the judgment sum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Resolution Management, or TADM, is mindful that workers should be able to recover their monies efficiently and cost-effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: TADM has partnered NTUC's U Care Centre and Migrant Workers' Centre to provide advice and assistance to local and migrant workers on enforcing ECT orders through a writ of seizure and sale (WSS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In cases where it may be impractical to proceed through a WSS, TADM will help affected workers get financial assistance through the Short-Term Relief Fund or the Migrant Workers' Assistance Fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Turning now, Sir, to the family justice system, it is a system that deals with many cases that are often less about legal issues and a lot about emotional and family issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Typically, this plays out in acrimonious, often protracted, proceedings, often souring the relations of people already strained by the proceedings themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Amendments to the Women's Charter this year were a step in this direction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng mentioned that family proceedings can be challenging for some litigants-in-person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He had asked today and also in a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on 15 February why many parties continue to choose to represent themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are, Sir, a variety of reasons for this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One factor could be the initiatives that MinLaw, together with MSF and FJC, have introduced, in fact, simplify and reduce the acrimony in divorce proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, we have implemented the simplified divorce track for couples who have agreed on the divorce and ancillary matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to simplify proceedings so that all parties can obtain a fair and just outcome even if they choose or are sometimes forced to go without a lawyer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some of the improvements we are, therefore, considering in the upcoming Bill will be especially helpful for self-represented parties, specifically, the enforcement of maintenance orders, which Dr Tan Wu Meng has spoken about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Take, for example, where the enforcing party has difficulty ascertaining the other party's financial position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, Members will know, is not an uncommon position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will empower the Courts to question parties and obtain the information directly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This facilitates a simpler and more efficient process and really gets to the crux of the issues directly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also considering additional enforcement mechanisms to strengthen compliance – a comment which Dr Tan Wu Meng had made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Vikram Nair suggested simplifying the enforcement process for ancillary orders made by a foreign court in divorce proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For fresh applications in Singapore for ancillary orders for foreign divorces, our Courts have been mindful to avoid unnecessary re-litigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Their approach is to respect and recognise any foreign custody order made in the child's habitual residence unless there are exceptional circumstances which militate against that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, Sir, we will consider Mr Vikram Nair's feedback.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai raised two matters on law reform and I will address those.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He commented on the Debtors Act dealing with arrest and imprisonment of debtors and asked if MinLaw would consider reviewing its relevance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about the recent Court of Appeal decision, which held that claims in unjust enrichment and restitution for wrongs are not covered by the Limitation Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, I think we had spoken about this with Mr Murali Pillai, and are studying, if we decide to proceed, how the Limitation Act should be amended.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to explore a range of possible refinements and, of course, also review our laws continually to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of our legal system and also ensure that justice continues to remain accessible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, Sir, access to justice is a fundamental pillar of our society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Advancing access to justice for all Singaporeans, regardless of their means, is, therefore, important to us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, community disputes remain an area of focus.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members have noted, there has been a rise in such cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An inter-agency committee comprising MCCY, MND, MinLaw and MHA has been working on a holistic review of the Community Disputes Management Framework, a broad holistic framework that looks at how we manage such disputes within the community from end to end as far as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The committee has made progress in this review.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst it is at this point in time premature to announce any firm measures at this stage, I can say that we are considering proposals and remedies which fall into two broad buckets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, to look at enhancing upstream measures to help reduce the occurrence of disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the committee is studying how we can forge closer relationships and partnership with the community to establish community norms for issues, such as noise and disturbances, local disamenity issues, and this includes the establishment of a community advisory panel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will elaborate on this during MND's Committee of Supply speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, if a dispute does arise, how can we enhance the framework to promote an amicable resolution as far as possible?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: After all, most of these disputes occur in the context of a neighbourly situation where two parties live side by side or in close proximity to each other.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How do we find a solution that better facilitates a fair, expedient and effective resolution of that dispute should an amicable resolution not be possible?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a complex effort, as Members would appreciate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It requires work and coordination amongst different agencies, and the committee has been working with stakeholders and partners to develop and refine these proposals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will share some further aspects of the committee's work at MCCY's Committee of Supply speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about efforts to reduce unclaimed CPF monies held by the Public Trustee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will recall that we are already simplifying the claims process through the beneficiary representative approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will apply to about half of all unnominated CPF monies handled by the Public Trustee annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We encourage beneficiaries who are able to, to use this process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The application process has also been streamlined, which will significantly reduce inconvenience for beneficiaries and also, in many cases, halve the disbursement time from the current three to six months to one to three months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also plan to review the monetary limit for cases to qualify under this approach, potentially expanding the approach to a larger group of cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The beneficiary representative approach will go some way towards reducing the inconvenience when making a claim for unclaimed unnominated sums and also reduce the unclaimed monies as a result.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I should add, however, that despite refining this and making it simpler and more convenient, that to enable distributions to beneficiaries more quickly and directly, CPF members can, where possible, make their nominations ahead of time and update it as their life circumstances change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, both Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested simplifying the probate process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last year, Members may recall that I had shared that the Courts are already working to simplify the application process for straightforward probate matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In gist, self-represented applicants can look forward to a probate e-service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can be used to apply for a Grant of Probate online in straightforward applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One key feature will be the integration of Singpass information, which will allow the applicant's particulars to be automatically populated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These features reduce the amount of information the applicant needs to provide and potential form-filling errors, which then lengthen and delay the process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will significantly improve the service journey for self-represented applicants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai raised an interesting proposal about the Japanese koseki system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is a system that has unique features.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Interesting, but, ultimately, we felt that it was relevant for Japan's own context – quite different from our situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We assessed that adopting it does not necessarily make Singapore's probate and administration processes more efficient and we felt that enhancing and making it more convenient and simplifying the process itself would benefit applicants more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, we take Mr Murali Pillai's suggestion and we are grateful that he has taken the trouble to look at comparable systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The lesson in that, really, is to look at other systems and think of how it may apply to us and adapt the process, as may be appropriate, to contextualise it to our circumstances, and we will do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai proposed reviewing the means test limit in order to strengthen access to justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has been less than three years since these criteria were revised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We should let this run for a period of time and study its impact and effectiveness before deciding whether to review the limits again.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Additionally, we also acknowledge Mr Murali	Pillai's suggestion on increasing awareness regarding the waiver of the means test requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We completely agree with that and we will take steps to enhance the awareness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will work with various other stakeholders, including Law Society, to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For those who lack resources but may not qualify for legal aid, Mr Vikram Nair asked whether conditional fee agreements (CFAs) could be expanded to domestic litigation and also include damages-based awards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will recall that Parliament passed a framework for CFAs in January.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are studying extending CFAs to other categories of proceedings – as I have explained when I made the speech in Parliament in January – such as in domestic litigation and mediation, in order to enhance access to justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are aware of the developments in this area in other jurisdictions like the UK and the US.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But as Members know, such proceedings are likely to involve more vulnerable litigants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we want to take this approach more carefully, study the pros and cons, make further reviews and consultations, before we move on this front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will, nonetheless, continue to study this and might have further consultations to study the appropriateness of such damages-based awards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The introduction of CFAs in its current form, nonetheless, will strengthen Singapore's offerings as a legal services and dispute resolution hub – a point that I will now turn to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It provides the necessary infrastructure for us to engage in commerce.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It contributes to Singapore's status as an international centre for finance, business, shipping, amongst others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore is building up its reputation as a legal and IP hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the Global Innovation Index 2021, Singapore was amongst the world's top 10 most innovative nations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how we will maintain Singapore as a dispute resolution hub amidst the changes brought about by the pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond updates to our laws, such as CFAs, that I mentioned, we continue to evolve our international commercial dispute offerings and infrastructure to meet the end-users and the parties' changing needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must evolve and move with the times and I am sure that what we offer, what we have in our jurisdiction, meets the needs of users of legal services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the pandemic, proceedings are now often held in an online or hybrid format.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our dispute resolution institutions moved quickly to offer online and hybrid solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will, therefore, work with them to consolidate these efforts, enhance their digital offerings at a broader level, and provide users with a comprehensive suite of online solutions and services, including hearing platforms and case management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also work with these institutions to expand their footprint into other jurisdictions and promote our services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes supporting this expansion overseas, as I have mentioned; strengthening cooperation with foreign counterparts in a mutually beneficial system; and stepping up our physical engagements with key stakeholders and target markets as travel resumes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how the profession will meet our evolving needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas talked about the high attrition rates, especially amongst young lawyers, and asked how we will support and retain talent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This phenomenon, however, is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An International Bar Association survey of more than 3,000 young lawyers globally published in January found that a third are likely to move to a new legal profession, for example, in academia; and a fifth are likely to leave the profession entirely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, that is about 20% likely to leave the profession entirely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They leave for a wide variety of reasons, including high workload and pressures, some of which the Members have mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But while there were lawyers who left the profession, the numbers of which I have cited, there were, equally, also new entrants and re-entrants into the profession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was also a net increase in the number of Practising Certificate (PC) holders, those who practise law, in 2021, compared to 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, overall, while there are a number of lawyers who have left the profession, equally, as I have said, others have come into the profession either at the start as a young lawyer or, in some cases, re-enter the profession as a mid-career or more senior lawyer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, I understand the sentiments of young lawyers and the views expressed by Members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both Mr Murali Pillai and myself, we practised together as young lawyers and we know the drill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first few years are when they go on a tremendously steep learning curve.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That helps them to deepen their knowledge, quicken their experience, hone their craft and gain exposure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With these challenges, they grow professionally and, I think, if truth be told, through this experience, they become better, more experienced, more well-rounded lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The reality, too, is that we need to be able to compete globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Otherwise, Singapore will be a less compelling proposition as a legal services hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is, therefore, no shortcut to developing legal skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is about the experience, it is about the ability to apply legal knowledge in the context of real-life, lived experiences, and make real commercial value judgements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If we want to be an outstanding legal hub and the jurisdiction of choice, there are no shortcuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we can make the journey more sustainable, more meaningful and rewarding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we will look into preparing our lawyers, especially young lawyers, more adequately for practice and, along the way, developments in practice throughout their careers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we will continue to provide lawyers with opportunities in the legal industry and the wider ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers today have more diverse options available, beyond joining as a lawyer in a Singapore law practice or joining the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, there are now opportunities at international law practices, in-house counsel teams, dispute resolution institutions, boutique firms and, of course, also legal tech firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are also more development opportunities within the Singapore law practices and the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our Singapore law practices second lawyers to partner firms and clients, including through programmes introduced by MinLaw.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Legal Service restructuring also gives opportunities to specialise in judicial roles or as public sector lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas suggested attracting more graduate students to read law, as they are more likely to stay in the profession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas might know that all three of our local law schools offer JD programmes and we see a healthy take-up every year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SUSS Law School, in particular, takes in more than 50% in each cohort of JD students on average.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, Sir, regardless of the law degree, lawyers will stay in the profession if there are opportunities and if they find the work fulfilling.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This requires the collective efforts of different stakeholders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will, therefore, continue to work with the Law Society and law practices to ensure that the legal industry remains attractive, challenging and with renewed opportunities for all and at the same time, continuing to foster a strong, talented, energetic Bar, with camaraderie among lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, let me turn to technology and digitalisation, as Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Christopher de Souza have raised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both have asked about supporting law practices and lawyers in the technology transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We launched a Technology and Innovation Roadmap in 2020, a 10-year roadmap to guide our efforts and direction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are working on a Legal Industry Digital Plan with IMDA and industry partners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a matters management tool that is integrated with technology tools popular with our lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It addresses common pain points when adopting and using technology, such as a steep learning curve and lack of interoperability between tools and systems, often a high threshold for lawyers to cross when talking about adopting technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also incorporating Singapore-specific features, features which we use best within our own local practice in our jurisdiction, including integration with existing practice management tools and solutions, and ensuring Singapore user data is hosted from Singapore, from a security perspective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have taken pains to ensure that user feedback is incorporated early into the design architecture of the system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the last year, we engaged over 100 lawyers from small and medium-sized law firms to obtain feedback on their usage, how they see interoperability, what functions they want to see, how they feel integration ought to take place between their own systems and the systems on the platform and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We established a standing LTP Industry Engagement & Advisory Group to provide continuous feedback as the product is developed and redeveloped over phases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We held a soft-launch at the end of January this year, where we provided a preview to some industry members and stakeholders, put the system with them and let them use it for a while, market test it, road test it before we finally make the launch later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Once launched, law firms will be able to start adoption progressively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw is working to ensure firms receive technology support as they adopt the platform and beyond.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will share more details of this closer to the launch.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, another area – intellectual property (IP) – which we see will carry Singapore into the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IP and intangible assets (IA) are engines of today’s innovation-driven global economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we have long recognised the need to leverage IA and IP for growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We encourage creation, protection and commercialisation of new innovations and technologies, including blockchain and other emerging digital technologies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rapid pace of innovation requires us to continually review our IP policies and laws to ensure that they support technological advances and, of course, the continually evolving business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how we are supporting local enterprises build infrastructure and monetise IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last year, we launched the Singapore IP Strategy 2030 (SIPS 2030).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This aims to strengthen Singapore as a top-ranked global IA/IP hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will touch on two areas, particularly relevant to local enterprises, given Mr Christopher de Souza's question.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the initiatives that enable enterprises to better leverage IA and IP for growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It allows patent applications to be granted as fast as six months and, in this area, Members will know, time is efficiency, efficiency is commercialisation and money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, as fast as six months, and the related trademark and design applications to be registered within three months and one month respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At IPOS’ complimentary IP Legal and Business Clinics, local enterprises can consult lawyers and business consultants on a range of IP matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since February, these Clinics offer advice on IP issues when expanding overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Concurrently, IPOS is working with Enterprise Singapore and the SME Centres to widen the IA/IP outreach to local enterprises, to socialise the idea with them, to equip them with information and knowledge, should they decide that their own business can take advantage of the IA/IP environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In May, IPOS will introduce the IPOS Digital Hub, a new IP registration system, which will harness the latest technologies to enhance the user experience in the IP registration process and provide businesses with new features to manage their own IP portfolio.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will complement the legislative updates in the Intellectual Property (Amendment) Bill passed in January 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Altogether, these initiatives will enable a more efficient and business-friendly IP registration system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are working on IA and IP disclosure and valuation to make IA and IP more recognised and also more transactable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS is working with ACRA and the industry to develop an Intangible Asset Disclosure Framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will enable enterprises to better identify, communicate and disclose the value of their IP and IA for growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We plan to consult the industry later this year, before introducing the Framework in 2023.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore will also work with international partners to develop internationally-recognised IA/IP valuation guidelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza recognises, optimising land resources is integral to sustaining Singapore’s economic and social development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It almost goes without saying that, given our limited land resources – this is an important piece of the puzzle to ensure that the land is optimised even as it awaits its next use – we manage our state land and properties carefully to ensure that they are put to the best possible use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In deciding how to utilise these assets, we consider not only economic returns, but also how they can bring broader societal benefits to the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To achieve this, we manage these assets along two broad thrusts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore Land Authority (SLA) has engaged extensively with market players to identify fresh concepts for existing state properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example is the upcoming rejuvenation of Gillman Barracks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will introduce creative lifestyle concepts to complement the existing commercial arts enclave and attract greater footfall.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Sustainability initiatives, such as green programmes and deployment of solar panels, will also be incorporated, as we do our part to grow the green movement in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, SLA will also be transforming the former campus of Loyang Primary School through adaptive reuse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first plot, a four-storey building, will be repurposed as a childcare centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA is working with potential tenants to introduce community elements to the adjacent plot with the aim of creating a synergistic community of complementary users within the same site.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These efforts, amongst others, will help to inject life into existing spaces in a manner that benefits both the business and the community, and keeps the use of state lands efficient and, of course, exciting and vibrant in the context of the community in which the state lands are situated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry will continue to forge ahead to ensure a trusted and efficient legal system, providing access to justice, regardless of means.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will strengthen our attractiveness as a legal and IP hub, a position that we have worked hard to gain, and which we must work even harder to maintain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue the stewardship of state properties and ensure our lived environment best serves Singaporeans’ needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I wish to thank the Judiciary, members of the Bar and of this House, Universities, law students and various agencies and professional institutions, including the Law Society and the Singapore Academy of Law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, we are fortunate to have an open and constructive relationship with all our stakeholders in the legal industry fraternity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have very robust but very constructive discussions, with a clear eye on what is best for Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are grateful for this, and look forward to extending our partnership and fostering new collaborations in the coming year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I also want to thank the many staff and officers of MinLaw who have spent much effort in ensuring that we achieve our objectives that I have set out in this speech.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened to know that an IA and IP international valuation framework or standard will be developed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I guess there are a lot of opportunities for the chartered accountants and auditors to work with the lawyers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I assure Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim that we will look at this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The system of law governing inheritance may be different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the administration is something that we can look at because both of the systems will require some degree of administration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The first is that Minister Edwin Tong talked quite a lot about therapeutic justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But I was wondering whether or not there could be some emphasis in the justice system on restorative justice, which is, reconciliation between parties, in addition to therapeutic justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For the second question, I declare that I am a lawyer in private practice and I do arbitrations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Be that as it may, may I ask what the Minister and MinLaw are doing to promote the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) rules, especially because arbitrations and hearings are increasingly being held via Zoom or online, so that the rules make all the difference to attract the case to SIAC?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the first question, the answer is yes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All the different objectives and principles behind what we do in sentencing will obviously apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the second query, yes, we have to ensure that we continue to put SIAC out there.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have to work hard at doing that, and part of this is also to ensure that SIAC remains in the mindshare.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, when we talk about forays into foreign jurisdictions, as we have done with Mr Murali Pillai, I think he was present on at least one of the trips overseas to speak about our rules, to talk about our system and to, basically, socialise the idea of using SIAC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that is one step that will be taken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, I think it is important to ensure that we continue to have the best arbitrators in SIAC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look at our Panel as one where we ensure that the best in the class, when it comes to arbitrators, are retained by SIAC – the best personnel, best expertise, best secretariat, to administer the cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are often the best advertisements, as it were, to ensure that parties, when they come to choosing the relevant rules, will come to choose SIAC rules and we can give them the best service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, as I mentioned in my speech, it is important to continually update our processes, our laws and even our procedures to ensure that we best fit the business use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we do this, when we make amendments like the CFA, for instance, we give parties out there the best reasons to come and use the SIAC and, in some cases also, be present in Singapore for the arbitration.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali Pillai, would you like to withdraw your amendment, please?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I would like to thank the hon Minister for his characteristic, comprehensive response to all the points raised in the hon Members' speeches.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, this year, I would not be wishing him and his officers as busy a year as last year, although from the plans that he has in mind, it seems to be going to be as busy, nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wish him and his officers well in the implementation of his plans to further the access to justice, strengthen the rule of law, grab the economic opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans and, of course, strengthen our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, Sir, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
